sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Why, she hath a face of her own.

sp.speaker: CURTIS
sp.p: Who knows not that?

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Thou, it seems, that calls for company to countenance her.

sp.speaker: CURTIS
sp.p: I call them forth to credit her.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Why, she comes to borrow nothing of them.

sp.speaker: NATHANIEL
sp.p: Welcome home, Grumio!

sp.speaker: PHILIP
sp.p: How now, Grumio!

sp.speaker: JOSEPH
sp.p: What, Grumio!

sp.speaker: NICHOLAS
sp.p: Fellow Grumio!

sp.speaker: NATHANIEL
sp.p: How now, old lad!

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Welcome, you; how now, you; what, you; fellow, you; and thus much for greeting. Now, my spruce companions, is all ready, and all things neat?

sp.speaker: NATHANIEL
sp.p: All things is ready. How near is our master?

lg.l: E’en at hand, alighted by this; and therefore be not,—
Cock’s passion, silence! I hear my master.
Where be these knaves? What! no man at door
To hold my stirrup nor to take my horse?
Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Philip?—

sp.speaker: ALL SERVANTS
sp.p: Here, here, sir; here, sir.

lg.l: Here, sir! here, sir! here, sir! here, sir!
You logger-headed and unpolish’d grooms!
What, no attendance? no regard? no duty?
Where is the foolish knave I sent before?

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Here, sir; as foolish as I was before.

lg.l: You peasant swain! you whoreson malt-horse drudge!
Did I not bid thee meet me in the park,
And bring along these rascal knaves with thee?
Nathaniel’s coat, sir, was not fully made,
And Gabriel’s pumps were all unpink’d i’ the heel;
There was no link to colour Peter’s hat,
And Walter’s dagger was not come from sheathing;
There was none fine but Adam, Ralph, and Gregory;
The rest were ragged, old, and beggarly;
Yet, as they are, here are they come to meet you.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Go, rascals, go and fetch my supper in.

div.p: Where is the life that late I led? Where are those—? Sit down, Kate, and welcome. Food, food, food, food!

Why, when, I say?—Nay, good sweet Kate, be merry.— Off with my boots, you rogues! you villains! when? It was the friar of orders grey, As he forth walked on his way: Out, you rogue! you pluck my foot awry:
Take that, and mend the plucking off the other. Be merry, Kate. Some water, here; what, ho! Where’s my spaniel Troilus? Sirrah, get you hence And bid my cousin Ferdinand come hither:
One, Kate, that you must kiss and be acquainted with. Where are my slippers? Shall I have some water? Come, Kate, and wash, and welcome heartily.—
div.stage: Servant lets the ewer fall. Petruchio strikes him.
div.p: You whoreson villain! will you let it fall?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Patience, I pray you; ’twas a fault unwilling.

lg.l: A whoreson, beetle-headed, flap-ear’d knave!
Come, Kate, sit down; I know you have a stomach.
Will you give thanks, sweet Kate, or else shall I?—
What’s this? Mutton?

sp.speaker: FIRST SERVANT
sp.p: Ay.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Who brought it?

sp.speaker: PETER
sp.p: I.

lg.l: ’Tis burnt; and so is all the meat.
What dogs are these! Where is the rascal cook?
How durst you, villains, bring it from the dresser,
And serve it thus to me that love it not?

div.stage: Throws the meat, etc., at them.
div.p: There, take it to you, trenchers, cups, and all. You heedless joltheads and unmanner’d slaves! What! do you grumble? I’ll be with you straight.

lg.l: I pray you, husband, be not so disquiet;
The meat was well, if you were so contented.
I tell thee, Kate, ’twas burnt and dried away,
And I expressly am forbid to touch it;
For it engenders choler, planteth anger;
And better ’twere that both of us did fast,
Since, of ourselves, ourselves are choleric,
Than feed it with such over-roasted flesh.
Be patient; tomorrow ’t shall be mended.
And for this night we’ll fast for company:
Come, I will bring thee to thy bridal chamber.

sp.speaker: NATHANIEL
sp.p: Peter, didst ever see the like?

sp.speaker: PETER
sp.p: He kills her in her own humour.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Where is he?

lg.l: In her chamber, making a sermon of continency to her;
And rails, and swears, and rates, that she, poor soul,
Knows not which way to stand, to look, to speak,
And sits as one new risen from a dream.
Away, away! for he is coming hither.
Thus have I politicly begun my reign,
And ’tis my hope to end successfully.
My falcon now is sharp and passing empty.
And till she stoop she must not be full-gorg’d,
For then she never looks upon her lure.
Another way I have to man my haggard,
To make her come, and know her keeper’s call,
That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites
That bate and beat, and will not be obedient.
She eat no meat today, nor none shall eat;
Last night she slept not, nor tonight she shall not;
As with the meat, some undeserved fault
I’ll find about the making of the bed;
And here I’ll fling the pillow, there the bolster,
This way the coverlet, another way the sheets;
Ay, and amid this hurly I intend
That all is done in reverend care of her;
And, in conclusion, she shall watch all night:
And if she chance to nod I’ll rail and brawl,
And with the clamour keep her still awake.
This is a way to kill a wife with kindness;
And thus I’ll curb her mad and headstrong humour.
He that knows better how to tame a shrew,
Now let him speak; ’tis charity to show.

div.head: SCENE II. Padua. Before Baptista’s house.

lg.l: Is ’t possible, friend Licio, that Mistress Bianca
Doth fancy any other but Lucentio?
I tell you, sir, she bears me fair in hand.
Sir, to satisfy you in what I have said,
Stand by and mark the manner of his teaching.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Now, mistress, profit you in what you read?

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: What, master, read you? First resolve me that.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: I read that I profess, The Art to Love.

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: And may you prove, sir, master of your art!

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: While you, sweet dear, prove mistress of my heart.

lg.l: Quick proceeders, marry! Now tell me, I pray,
You that durst swear that your Mistress Bianca
Lov’d none in the world so well as Lucentio.
O despiteful love! unconstant womankind!
I tell thee, Licio, this is wonderful.
Mistake no more; I am not Licio.
Nor a musician as I seem to be;
But one that scorn to live in this disguise
For such a one as leaves a gentleman
And makes a god of such a cullion:
Know, sir, that I am call’d Hortensio.
Signior Hortensio, I have often heard
Of your entire affection to Bianca;
And since mine eyes are witness of her lightness,
I will with you, if you be so contented,
Forswear Bianca and her love for ever.
See, how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio,
Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow
Never to woo her more, but do forswear her,
As one unworthy all the former favours
That I have fondly flatter’d her withal.
And here I take the like unfeigned oath,
Never to marry with her though she would entreat;
Fie on her! See how beastly she doth court him!
Would all the world but he had quite forsworn!
For me, that I may surely keep mine oath,
I will be married to a wealthy widow
Ere three days pass, which hath as long lov’d me
As I have lov’d this proud disdainful haggard.
And so farewell, Signior Lucentio.
Kindness in women, not their beauteous looks,
Shall win my love; and so I take my leave,
In resolution as I swore before.

div.stage: Exit Hortensio. Lucentio and Bianca advance.

lg.l: Mistress Bianca, bless you with such grace
As ’longeth to a lover’s blessed case!
Nay, I have ta’en you napping, gentle love,
And have forsworn you with Hortensio.

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: Tranio, you jest; but have you both forsworn me?

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Mistress, we have.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Then we are rid of Licio.

lg.l: I’ faith, he’ll have a lusty widow now,
That shall be woo’d and wedded in a day.

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: God give him joy!

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Ay, and he’ll tame her.

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: He says so, Tranio.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Faith, he is gone unto the taming-school.

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: The taming-school! What, is there such a place?

lg.l: Ay, mistress; and Petruchio is the master,
That teacheth tricks eleven and twenty long,
To tame a shrew and charm her chattering tongue.
O master, master! I have watch’d so long
That I am dog-weary; but at last I spied
An ancient angel coming down the hill
Will serve the turn.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: What is he, Biondello?

lg.l: Master, a mercatante or a pedant,
I know not what; but formal in apparel,
In gait and countenance surely like a father.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: And what of him, Tranio?

lg.l: If he be credulous and trust my tale,
I’ll make him glad to seem Vincentio,
And give assurance to Baptista Minola,
As if he were the right Vincentio.
Take in your love, and then let me alone.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: God save you, sir!

lg.l: And you, sir! you are welcome.
Travel you far on, or are you at the farthest?
Sir, at the farthest for a week or two;
But then up farther, and as far as Rome;
And so to Tripoli, if God lend me life.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: What countryman, I pray?

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Of Mantua.

lg.l: Of Mantua, sir? Marry, God forbid,
And come to Padua, careless of your life!

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: My life, sir! How, I pray? for that goes hard.

lg.l: ’Tis death for anyone in Mantua
To come to Padua. Know you not the cause?
Your ships are stay’d at Venice; and the Duke,—
For private quarrel ’twixt your Duke and him,—
Hath publish’d and proclaim’d it openly.
’Tis marvel, but that you are but newly come
You might have heard it else proclaim’d about.
Alas, sir! it is worse for me than so;
For I have bills for money by exchange
From Florence, and must here deliver them.
Well, sir, to do you courtesy,
This will I do, and this I will advise you:
First, tell me, have you ever been at Pisa?
Ay, sir, in Pisa have I often been,
Pisa renowned for grave citizens.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Among them know you one Vincentio?

lg.l: I know him not, but I have heard of him,
A merchant of incomparable wealth.
He is my father, sir; and, sooth to say,
In countenance somewhat doth resemble you.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Aside. As much as an apple doth an oyster, and all one.

lg.l: To save your life in this extremity,
This favour will I do you for his sake;
And think it not the worst of all your fortunes
That you are like to Sir Vincentio.
His name and credit shall you undertake,
And in my house you shall be friendly lodg’d;
Look that you take upon you as you should!
You understand me, sir; so shall you stay
Till you have done your business in the city.
If this be courtesy, sir, accept of it.
O, sir, I do; and will repute you ever
The patron of my life and liberty.
Then go with me to make the matter good.
This, by the way, I let you understand:
My father is here look’d for every day
To pass assurance of a dower in marriage
’Twixt me and one Baptista’s daughter here:
In all these circumstances I’ll instruct you.
Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.

div.head: SCENE III. A room in Petruchio’s house.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: No, no, forsooth; I dare not for my life.

lg.l: The more my wrong, the more his spite appears.
What, did he marry me to famish me?
Beggars that come unto my father’s door
Upon entreaty have a present alms;
If not, elsewhere they meet with charity;
But I, who never knew how to entreat,
Nor never needed that I should entreat,
Am starv’d for meat, giddy for lack of sleep;
With oaths kept waking, and with brawling fed.
And that which spites me more than all these wants,
He does it under name of perfect love;
As who should say, if I should sleep or eat
’Twere deadly sickness, or else present death.
I prithee go and get me some repast;
I care not what, so it be wholesome food.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: What say you to a neat’s foot?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: ’Tis passing good; I prithee let me have it.

lg.l: I fear it is too choleric a meat.
How say you to a fat tripe finely broil’d?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: I like it well; good Grumio, fetch it me.

lg.l: I cannot tell; I fear ’tis choleric.
What say you to a piece of beef and mustard?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: A dish that I do love to feed upon.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Why then the beef, and let the mustard rest.

lg.l: Nay, then I will not: you shall have the mustard,
Or else you get no beef of Grumio.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Then both, or one, or anything thou wilt.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Why then the mustard without the beef.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave,

div.p: That feed’st me with the very name of meat. Sorrow on thee and all the pack of you That triumph thus upon my misery! Go, get thee gone, I say.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio with a dish of meat; and Hortensio.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Mistress, what cheer?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Faith, as cold as can be.

lg.l: Pluck up thy spirits; look cheerfully upon me.
Here, love; thou seest how diligent I am,
To dress thy meat myself, and bring it thee:

div.stage: Sets the dish on a table.
div.p: I am sure, sweet Kate, this kindness merits thanks. What! not a word? Nay, then thou lov’st it not, And all my pains is sorted to no proof. Here, take away this dish.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: I pray you, let it stand.

lg.l: The poorest service is repaid with thanks;
And so shall mine, before you touch the meat.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: I thank you, sir.

lg.l: Signior Petruchio, fie! you are to blame.
Come, Mistress Kate, I’ll bear you company.
Aside. Eat it up all, Hortensio, if thou lovest me.
Much good do it unto thy gentle heart!
Kate, eat apace: and now, my honey love,
Will we return unto thy father’s house
And revel it as bravely as the best,
With silken coats and caps, and golden rings,
With ruffs and cuffs and farthingales and things;
With scarfs and fans and double change of bravery,
With amber bracelets, beads, and all this knavery.
What! hast thou din’d? The tailor stays thy leisure,
To deck thy body with his ruffling treasure.

div.p: Come, tailor, let us see these ornaments; Lay forth the gown.—
What news with you, sir?

sp.speaker: HABERDASHER
sp.p: Here is the cap your worship did bespeak.

lg.l: Why, this was moulded on a porringer;
A velvet dish: fie, fie! ’tis lewd and filthy:
Why, ’tis a cockle or a walnut-shell,
A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby’s cap:
Away with it! come, let me have a bigger.
I’ll have no bigger; this doth fit the time,
And gentlewomen wear such caps as these.
When you are gentle, you shall have one too,
And not till then.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Aside That will not be in haste.

lg.l: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak;
And speak I will. I am no child, no babe.
Your betters have endur’d me say my mind,
And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
My tongue will tell the anger of my heart,
Or else my heart, concealing it, will break;
And rather than it shall, I will be free
Even to the uttermost, as I please, in words.
Why, thou say’st true; it is a paltry cap,
A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie;
I love thee well in that thou lik’st it not.
Love me or love me not, I like the cap;
And it I will have, or I will have none.
Thy gown? Why, ay: come, tailor, let us see’t.
O mercy, God! what masquing stuff is here?
What’s this? A sleeve? ’Tis like a demi-cannon.
What, up and down, carv’d like an apple tart?
Here’s snip and nip and cut and slish and slash,
Like to a censer in a barber’s shop.
Why, what i’ devil’s name, tailor, call’st thou this?

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Aside I see she’s like to have neither cap nor gown.

lg.l: You bid me make it orderly and well,
According to the fashion and the time.
Marry, and did; but if you be remember’d,
I did not bid you mar it to the time.
Go, hop me over every kennel home,
For you shall hop without my custom, sir.
I’ll none of it: hence! make your best of it.
I never saw a better fashion’d gown,
More quaint, more pleasing, nor more commendable;
Belike you mean to make a puppet of me.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Why, true; he means to make a puppet of thee.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: She says your worship means to make a puppet of her.

lg.l: O monstrous arrogance! Thou liest, thou thread,
Thou thimble,
Thou yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail!
Thou flea, thou nit, thou winter-cricket thou!
Brav’d in mine own house with a skein of thread!
Away! thou rag, thou quantity, thou remnant,
Or I shall so be-mete thee with thy yard
As thou shalt think on prating whilst thou liv’st!
I tell thee, I, that thou hast marr’d her gown.
Your worship is deceiv’d: the gown is made
Just as my master had direction.
Grumio gave order how it should be done.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: I gave him no order; I gave him the stuff.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: But how did you desire it should be made?

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Marry, sir, with needle and thread.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: But did you not request to have it cut?

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Thou hast faced many things.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: I have.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Face not me. Thou hast braved many men; brave not me: I will neither be fac’d nor brav’d. I say unto thee, I bid thy master cut out the gown; but I did not bid him cut it to pieces: ergo, thou liest.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: Why, here is the note of the fashion to testify.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Read it.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: The note lies in ’s throat, if he say I said so.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: ’Imprimis, a loose-bodied gown.’

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Master, if ever I said loose-bodied gown, sew me in the skirts of it and beat me to death with a bottom of brown thread; I said, a gown.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Proceed.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: ‘With a small compassed cape.’

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: I confess the cape.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: ‘With a trunk sleeve.’

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: I confess two sleeves.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: ‘The sleeves curiously cut.’

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Ay, there’s the villainy.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Error i’ the bill, sir; error i’ the bill. I commanded the sleeves should be cut out, and sew’d up again; and that I’ll prove upon thee, though thy little finger be armed in a thimble.

sp.speaker: TAILOR
sp.p: This is true that I say; and I had thee in place where thou shouldst know it.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: I am for thee straight; take thou the bill, give me thy mete-yard, and spare not me.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: God-a-mercy, Grumio! Then he shall have no odds.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: You are i’ the right, sir; ’tis for my mistress.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Go, take it up unto thy master’s use.

sp.speaker: GRUMIO
sp.p: Villain, not for thy life! Take up my mistress’ gown for thy master’s use!

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Why, sir, what’s your conceit in that?

lg.l: O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think for.
Take up my mistress’ gown to his master’s use!
O fie, fie, fie!
Aside Hortensio, say thou wilt see the tailor paid.
To Tailor. Go take it hence; be gone, and say no more.
Aside to Tailor. Tailor, I’ll pay thee for thy gown tomorrow;
Take no unkindness of his hasty words.
Away, I say! commend me to thy master.
Well, come, my Kate; we will unto your father’s
Even in these honest mean habiliments.
Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor
For ’tis the mind that makes the body rich;
And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds,
So honour peereth in the meanest habit.
What, is the jay more precious than the lark
Because his feathers are more beautiful?
Or is the adder better than the eel
Because his painted skin contents the eye?
O no, good Kate; neither art thou the worse
For this poor furniture and mean array.
If thou account’st it shame, lay it on me;
And therefore frolic; we will hence forthwith,
To feast and sport us at thy father’s house.
Go call my men, and let us straight to him;
And bring our horses unto Long-lane end;
There will we mount, and thither walk on foot.
Let’s see; I think ’tis now some seven o’clock,
And well we may come there by dinner-time.
I dare assure you, sir, ’tis almost two,
And ’twill be supper-time ere you come there.
It shall be seven ere I go to horse.
Look what I speak, or do, or think to do,
You are still crossing it. Sirs, let ’t alone:
I will not go today; and ere I do,
It shall be what o’clock I say it is.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Why, so this gallant will command the sun.

div.head: SCENE IV. Padua. Before Baptista’s house.
div.stage: Enter Tranio and the Pedant dressed like Vincentio

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Sir, this is the house; please it you that I call?

lg.l: Ay, what else? and, but I be deceived,
Signior Baptista may remember me,
Near twenty years ago in Genoa,
Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.
’Tis well; and hold your own, in any case,
With such austerity as ’longeth to a father.
I warrant you. But, sir, here comes your boy;
’Twere good he were school’d.
Fear you not him. Sirrah Biondello,
Now do your duty throughly, I advise you.
Imagine ’twere the right Vincentio.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Tut! fear not me.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista?

lg.l: I told him that your father was at Venice,
And that you look’d for him this day in Padua.
Th’art a tall fellow; hold thee that to drink.
Here comes Baptista. Set your countenance, sir.

div.p: Signior Baptista, you are happily met. To the Pedant Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of; I pray you stand good father to me now; Give me Bianca for my patrimony.

lg.l: Soft, son!
Sir, by your leave: having come to Padua
To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio
Made me acquainted with a weighty cause
Of love between your daughter and himself:
And,—for the good report I hear of you,
And for the love he beareth to your daughter,
And she to him,—to stay him not too long,
I am content, in a good father’s care,
To have him match’d; and, if you please to like
No worse than I, upon some agreement
Me shall you find ready and willing
With one consent to have her so bestow’d;
For curious I cannot be with you,
Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.
Sir, pardon me in what I have to say.
Your plainness and your shortness please me well.
Right true it is your son Lucentio here
Doth love my daughter, and she loveth him,
Or both dissemble deeply their affections;
And therefore, if you say no more than this,
That like a father you will deal with him,
And pass my daughter a sufficient dower,
The match is made, and all is done:
Your son shall have my daughter with consent.
I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best
We be affied, and such assurance ta’en
As shall with either part’s agreement stand?
Not in my house, Lucentio, for you know
Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants;
Besides, old Gremio is hearkening still,
And happily we might be interrupted.
Then at my lodging, and it like you:
There doth my father lie; and there this night
We’ll pass the business privately and well.
Send for your daughter by your servant here;
My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently.
The worst is this, that at so slender warning
You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.
It likes me well. Cambio, hie you home,
And bid Bianca make her ready straight;
And, if you will, tell what hath happened:
Lucentio’s father is arriv’d in Padua,
And how she’s like to be Lucentio’s wife.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: I pray the gods she may, with all my heart!

lg.l: Dally not with the gods, but get thee gone.
Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way?
Welcome! One mess is like to be your cheer;
Come, sir; we will better it in Pisa.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: I follow you.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Cambio!

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: What say’st thou, Biondello?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: You saw my master wink and laugh upon you?

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Biondello, what of that?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Faith, nothing; but has left me here behind to expound the meaning or moral of his signs and tokens.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: I pray thee moralize them.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Then thus: Baptista is safe, talking with the deceiving father of a deceitful son.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: And what of him?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: And then?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: The old priest at Saint Luke’s church is at your command at all hours.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: And what of all this?

lg.l: I cannot tell, except they are busied about a counterfeit assurance. Take your assurance of her, cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum; to the church! take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient honest witnesses.
If this be not that you look for, I have more to say,
But bid Bianca farewell for ever and a day.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Hear’st thou, Biondello?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: I cannot tarry: I knew a wench married in an afternoon as she went to the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit; and so may you, sir; and so adieu, sir. My master hath appointed me to go to Saint Luke’s to bid the priest be ready to come against you come with your appendix.

lg.l: I may, and will, if she be so contented.
She will be pleas’d; then wherefore should I doubt?
Hap what hap may, I’ll roundly go about her;
It shall go hard if Cambio go without her:

div.head: SCENE V. A public road.
div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Katherina, Hortensio and Servants.

lg.l: Come on, i’ God’s name; once more toward our father’s.
Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: The moon! The sun; it is not moonlight now.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: I say it is the moon that shines so bright.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: I know it is the sun that shines so bright.

lg.l: Now by my mother’s son, and that’s myself,
It shall be moon, or star, or what I list,
Or ere I journey to your father’s house.
Go on and fetch our horses back again.
Evermore cross’d and cross’d; nothing but cross’d!

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Say as he says, or we shall never go.

lg.l: Forward, I pray, since we have come so far,
And be it moon, or sun, or what you please;
And if you please to call it a rush-candle,
Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: I say it is the moon.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: I know it is the moon.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Nay, then you lie; it is the blessed sun.

lg.l: Then, God be bless’d, it is the blessed sun;
But sun it is not when you say it is not,
And the moon changes even as your mind.
What you will have it nam’d, even that it is,
And so it shall be so for Katherine.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Petruchio, go thy ways; the field is won.

lg.l: Well, forward, forward! thus the bowl should run,
And not unluckily against the bias.
But, soft! Company is coming here.

div.stage: Enter Vincentio, in a travelling dress.
div.p: To Vincentio Good morrow, gentle mistress; where away? Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly too, Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman? Such war of white and red within her cheeks! What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty As those two eyes become that heavenly face? Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee. Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty’s sake.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: A will make the man mad, to make a woman of him.

lg.l: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet,
Whither away, or where is thy abode?
Happy the parents of so fair a child;
Happier the man whom favourable stars
Allot thee for his lovely bedfellow.
Why, how now, Kate! I hope thou art not mad:
This is a man, old, wrinkled, faded, wither’d,
And not a maiden, as thou sayst he is.
Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes,
That have been so bedazzled with the sun
That everything I look on seemeth green:
Now I perceive thou art a reverend father;
Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.
Do, good old grandsire, and withal make known
Which way thou travellest: if along with us,
We shall be joyful of thy company.
Fair sir, and you my merry mistress,
That with your strange encounter much amaz’d me,
My name is called Vincentio; my dwelling Pisa;
And bound I am to Padua, there to visit
A son of mine, which long I have not seen.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: What is his name?

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Lucentio, gentle sir.

lg.l: Happily met; the happier for thy son.
And now by law, as well as reverend age,
I may entitle thee my loving father:
The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman,
Thy son by this hath married. Wonder not,
Nor be not griev’d: she is of good esteem,
Her dowry wealthy, and of worthy birth;
Beside, so qualified as may beseem
The spouse of any noble gentleman.
Let me embrace with old Vincentio;
And wander we to see thy honest son,
Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.
But is this true? or is it else your pleasure,
Like pleasant travellers, to break a jest
Upon the company you overtake?

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: I do assure thee, father, so it is.

lg.l: Come, go along, and see the truth hereof;
For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.
Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart.
Have to my widow! and if she be froward,
Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.

div.head: ACT V
SCENE I. Padua. Before Lucentio’s house.
div.stage: Enter on one side Biondello, Lucentio and Bianca; Gremio walking on other side.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Softly and swiftly, sir, for the priest is ready.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: I fly, Biondello; but they may chance to need thee at home, therefore leave us.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Nay, faith, I’ll see the church o’ your back; and then come back to my master’s as soon as I can.

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.

div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Katherina, Vincentio and Attendants.

lg.l: Sir, here’s the door; this is Lucentio’s house:
My father’s bears more toward the market-place;
Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.
You shall not choose but drink before you go.
I think I shall command your welcome here,
And by all likelihood some cheer is toward.

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: They’re busy within; you were best knock louder.

div.stage: Enter Pedant above, at a window.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: What’s he that knocks as he would beat down the gate?

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Is Signior Lucentio within, sir?

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: He’s within, sir, but not to be spoken withal.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two to make merry withal?

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Keep your hundred pounds to yourself: he shall need none so long as I live.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Nay, I told you your son was well beloved in Padua. Do you hear, sir? To leave frivolous circumstances, I pray you tell Signior Lucentio that his father is come from Pisa, and is here at the door to speak with him.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Thou liest: his father is come from Padua, and here looking out at the window.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Art thou his father?

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Ay, sir; so his mother says, if I may believe her.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: To Vincentio Why, how now, gentleman! why, this is flat knavery to take upon you another man’s name.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Lay hands on the villain: I believe a means to cozen somebody in this city under my countenance.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: I have seen them in the church together: God send ’em good shipping! But who is here? Mine old master, Vincentio! Now we are undone and brought to nothing.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Seeing Biondello. Come hither, crack-hemp.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: I hope I may choose, sir.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Come hither, you rogue. What, have you forgot me?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Forgot you! No, sir: I could not forget you, for I never saw you before in all my life.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: What, you notorious villain! didst thou never see thy master’s father, Vincentio?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: What, my old worshipful old master? Yes, marry, sir; see where he looks out of the window.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Is’t so, indeed?

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: Help, help, help! here’s a madman will murder me.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Help, son! help, Signior Baptista!

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Prithee, Kate, let’s stand aside and see the end of this controversy.

div.stage: Re-enter Pedant, below; Baptista, Tranio and Servants.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Sir, what are you that offer to beat my servant?

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: What am I, sir! nay, what are you, sir? O immortal gods! O fine villain! A silken doublet, a velvet hose, a scarlet cloak, and a copatain hat! O, I am undone! I am undone! While I play the good husband at home, my son and my servant spend all at the university.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: How now! what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: What, is the man lunatic?

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Sir, you seem a sober ancient gentleman by your habit, but your words show you a madman. Why, sir, what ’cerns it you if I wear pearl and gold? I thank my good father, I am able to maintain it.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Thy father! O villain! he is a sailmaker in Bergamo.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: You mistake, sir; you mistake, sir. Pray, what do you think is his name?

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: His name! As if I knew not his name! I have brought him up ever since he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Away, away, mad ass! His name is Lucentio; and he is mine only son, and heir to the lands of me, Signior Vincentio.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Lucentio! O, he hath murdered his master! Lay hold on him, I charge you, in the Duke’s name. O, my son, my son! Tell me, thou villain, where is my son, Lucentio?

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Call forth an officer.

div.p: Carry this mad knave to the gaol. Father Baptista, I charge you see that he be forthcoming.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Carry me to the gaol!

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: Stay, officer; he shall not go to prison.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: Talk not, Signior Gremio; I say he shall go to prison.

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be cony-catched in this business; I dare swear this is the right Vincentio.

sp.speaker: PEDANT
sp.p: Swear if thou darest.

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: Nay, I dare not swear it.

sp.speaker: TRANIO
sp.p: Then thou wert best say that I am not Lucentio.

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: Away with the dotard! to the gaol with him!

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Thus strangers may be haled and abus’d: O monstrous villain!

div.stage: Re-enter Biondello, with Lucentio and Bianca.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: O! we are spoiled; and yonder he is: deny him, forswear him, or else we are all undone.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Kneeling. Pardon, sweet father.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Lives my sweetest son?

div.stage: Biondello, Tranio and Pedant run out.

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: Kneeling. Pardon, dear father.

lg.l: How hast thou offended?
Where is Lucentio?
Here’s Lucentio,
Right son to the right Vincentio;
That have by marriage made thy daughter mine,
While counterfeit supposes blear’d thine eyne.

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: Here ’s packing, with a witness, to deceive us all!

lg.l: Where is that damned villain, Tranio,
That fac’d and brav’d me in this matter so?

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: Cambio is chang’d into Lucentio.

lg.l: Love wrought these miracles. Bianca’s love
Made me exchange my state with Tranio,
While he did bear my countenance in the town;
And happily I have arriv’d at the last
Unto the wished haven of my bliss.
What Tranio did, myself enforc’d him to;
Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: I’ll slit the villain’s nose that would have sent me to the gaol.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: To Lucentio. But do you hear, sir? Have you married my daughter without asking my good will?

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Fear not, Baptista; we will content you, go to: but I will in, to be revenged for this villainy.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: And I to sound the depth of this knavery.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Look not pale, Bianca; thy father will not frown.

lg.l: My cake is dough, but I’ll in among the rest;
Out of hope of all but my share of the feast.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Husband, let’s follow to see the end of this ado.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: First kiss me, Kate, and we will.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: What! in the midst of the street?

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: What! art thou ashamed of me?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: No, sir; God forbid; but ashamed to kiss.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Why, then, let’s home again. Come, sirrah, let’s away.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay.

lg.l: Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate:
Better once than never, for never too late.

div.head: SCENE II. A room in Lucentio’s house.
div.stage: Enter Baptista, Vincentio, Gremio, the Pedant, Lucentio, Bianca, Petruchio, Katherina, Hortensio and Widow. Tranio, Biondello and Grumio and Others, attending.

lg.l: At last, though long, our jarring notes agree:
And time it is when raging war is done,
To smile at ’scapes and perils overblown.
My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome,
While I with self-same kindness welcome thine.
Brother Petruchio, sister Katherina,
And thou, Hortensio, with thy loving widow,
Feast with the best, and welcome to my house:
My banquet is to close our stomachs up,
After our great good cheer. Pray you, sit down;
For now we sit to chat as well as eat.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: Padua affords this kindness, son Petruchio.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Padua affords nothing but what is kind.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: For both our sakes I would that word were true.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Now, for my life, Hortensio fears his widow.

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: Then never trust me if I be afeard.

lg.l: You are very sensible, and yet you miss my sense:
I mean Hortensio is afeard of you.

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: He that is giddy thinks the world turns round.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Roundly replied.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: Mistress, how mean you that?

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: Thus I conceive by him.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Conceives by me! How likes Hortensio that?

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: My widow says thus she conceives her tale.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Very well mended. Kiss him for that, good widow.

lg.l: ’He that is giddy thinks the world turns round’:
I pray you tell me what you meant by that.
Your husband, being troubled with a shrew,
Measures my husband’s sorrow by his woe;
And now you know my meaning.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: A very mean meaning.

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: Right, I mean you.

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: And I am mean, indeed, respecting you.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: To her, Kate!

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: To her, widow!

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: That’s my office.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Spoke like an officer: ha’ to thee, lad.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: How likes Gremio these quick-witted folks?

sp.speaker: GREMIO
sp.p: Believe me, sir, they butt together well.

lg.l: Head and butt! An hasty-witted body
Would say your head and butt were head and horn.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: Ay, mistress bride, hath that awaken’d you?

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: Ay, but not frighted me; therefore I’ll sleep again.

lg.l: Nay, that you shall not; since you have begun,
Have at you for a bitter jest or two.
Am I your bird? I mean to shift my bush,
And then pursue me as you draw your bow.
You are welcome all.
She hath prevented me. Here, Signior Tranio;
This bird you aim’d at, though you hit her not:
Therefore a health to all that shot and miss’d.
O, sir! Lucentio slipp’d me like his greyhound,
Which runs himself, and catches for his master.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: A good swift simile, but something currish.

lg.l: ’Tis well, sir, that you hunted for yourself:
’Tis thought your deer does hold you at a bay.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: O ho, Petruchio! Tranio hits you now.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Confess, confess; hath he not hit you here?

lg.l: A has a little gall’d me, I confess;
And as the jest did glance away from me,
’Tis ten to one it maim’d you two outright.
Now, in good sadness, son Petruchio,
I think thou hast the veriest shrew of all.
Well, I say no; and therefore, for assurance,
Let’s each one send unto his wife,
And he whose wife is most obedient,
To come at first when he doth send for her,
Shall win the wager which we will propose.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Content. What’s the wager?

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Twenty crowns.

lg.l: Twenty crowns!
I’ll venture so much of my hawk or hound,
But twenty times so much upon my wife.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: A hundred then.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Content.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: A match! ’tis done.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Who shall begin?

lg.l: That will I.
Go, Biondello, bid your mistress come to me.

sp.speaker: BIONDELLO
sp.p: I go.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: Son, I’ll be your half, Bianca comes.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: I’ll have no halves; I’ll bear it all myself.

div.p: How now! what news?

lg.l: Sir, my mistress sends you word
That she is busy and she cannot come.
How! She’s busy, and she cannot come!
Is that an answer?
Ay, and a kind one too:
Pray God, sir, your wife send you not a worse.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: I hope better.

lg.l: Sirrah Biondello, go and entreat my wife
To come to me forthwith.
O, ho! entreat her!
Nay, then she must needs come.
I am afraid, sir,
Do what you can, yours will not be entreated.

div.p: Now, where’s my wife?

lg.l: She says you have some goodly jest in hand:
She will not come; she bids you come to her.
Worse and worse; she will not come! O vile,
Intolerable, not to be endur’d!
Sirrah Grumio, go to your mistress,
Say I command her come to me.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: I know her answer.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: She will not.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: The fouler fortune mine, and there an end.

sp.speaker: BAPTISTA
sp.p: Now, by my holidame, here comes Katherina!

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: What is your will sir, that you send for me?

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Where is your sister, and Hortensio’s wife?

sp.speaker: KATHERINA
sp.p: They sit conferring by the parlour fire.

lg.l: Go fetch them hither; if they deny to come,
Swinge me them soundly forth unto their husbands.
Away, I say, and bring them hither straight.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Here is a wonder, if you talk of a wonder.

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: And so it is. I wonder what it bodes.

lg.l: Marry, peace it bodes, and love, and quiet life,
An awful rule, and right supremacy;
And, to be short, what not that’s sweet and happy.
Now fair befall thee, good Petruchio!
The wager thou hast won; and I will add
Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns;
Another dowry to another daughter,
For she is chang’d, as she had never been.
Nay, I will win my wager better yet,
And show more sign of her obedience,
Her new-built virtue and obedience.
See where she comes, and brings your froward wives
As prisoners to her womanly persuasion.

div.stage: Re-enter Katherina with Bianca and Widow.
div.p: Katherine, that cap of yours becomes you not: Off with that bauble, throw it underfoot.
div.stage: Katherina pulls off her cap and throws it down.

lg.l: Lord, let me never have a cause to sigh
Till I be brought to such a silly pass!

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: Fie! what a foolish duty call you this?

lg.l: I would your duty were as foolish too;
The wisdom of your duty, fair Bianca,
Hath cost me a hundred crowns since supper-time!

sp.speaker: BIANCA
sp.p: The more fool you for laying on my duty.

lg.l: Katherine, I charge thee, tell these headstrong women
What duty they do owe their lords and husbands.

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: Come, come, you’re mocking; we will have no telling.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Come on, I say; and first begin with her.

sp.speaker: WIDOW
sp.p: She shall not.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: I say she shall: and first begin with her.

lg.l: Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow,
And dart not scornful glances from those eyes
To wound thy lord, thy king, thy governor:
It blots thy beauty as frosts do bite the meads,
Confounds thy fame as whirlwinds shake fair buds,
And in no sense is meet or amiable.
A woman mov’d is like a fountain troubled,
Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty;
And while it is so, none so dry or thirsty
Will deign to sip or touch one drop of it.
Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper,
Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee,
And for thy maintenance commits his body
To painful labour both by sea and land,
To watch the night in storms, the day in cold,
Whilst thou liest warm at home, secure and safe;
And craves no other tribute at thy hands
But love, fair looks, and true obedience;
Too little payment for so great a debt.
Such duty as the subject owes the prince,
Even such a woman oweth to her husband;
And when she is froward, peevish, sullen, sour,
And not obedient to his honest will,
What is she but a foul contending rebel
And graceless traitor to her loving lord?—
I am asham’d that women are so simple
To offer war where they should kneel for peace,
Or seek for rule, supremacy, and sway,
When they are bound to serve, love, and obey.
Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth,
Unapt to toil and trouble in the world,
But that our soft conditions and our hearts
Should well agree with our external parts?
Come, come, you froward and unable worms!
My mind hath been as big as one of yours,
My heart as great, my reason haply more,
To bandy word for word and frown for frown;
But now I see our lances are but straws,
Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare,
That seeming to be most which we indeed least are.
Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot,
And place your hands below your husband’s foot:
In token of which duty, if he please,
My hand is ready; may it do him ease.

sp.speaker: PETRUCHIO
sp.p: Why, there’s a wench! Come on, and kiss me, Kate.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: Well, go thy ways, old lad, for thou shalt ha’t.

sp.speaker: VINCENTIO
sp.p: ’Tis a good hearing when children are toward.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: But a harsh hearing when women are froward.

lg.l: Come, Kate, we’ll to bed.
We three are married, but you two are sped.
’Twas I won the wager,
To Lucentio. though you hit the white;
And being a winner, God give you good night!

sp.speaker: HORTENSIO
sp.p: Now go thy ways; thou hast tam’d a curst shrew.

sp.speaker: LUCENTIO
sp.p: ’Tis a wonder, by your leave, she will be tam’d so.
